domains.title: Renowned Little Prince
domains.subtitle: Healer, Sake-Maker, and Shaper of the Land
domains.lead: Sukunahikona is a tiny kami with enormous power. Floating to Japan in a boat of bark, he met Ōkuninushi and helped him pacify and cultivate the land. He taught the arts of healing and sake-making, and he became a protector against smallpox and illness. His small size makes him a deity of the overlooked and the underestimated.

mythology.lead: Sukunahikona's mythology in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki emphasizes that size and power are not the same.

myths.title: Arrival in a Bark Boat
myths.text: Sukunahikona arrived in Japan from the land of Tokoyo in a boat made of bark. He met Ōkuninushi, who recognized his power despite his small size. Together they traveled the land, pacifying spirits, establishing boundaries, and making the world fit for human habitation.

myths.title: Healer and Brewer
myths.text: Sukunahikona taught the arts of healing and sake-making. When illness struck, his knowledge saved the people. His association with smallpox made him a protective deity invoked during epidemics, and his sake became the offering that eased communication between humans and kami.

myths.title: Disappearance
myths.text: After completing his work, Sukunahikona crossed to the land of Tokoyo, the eternal land across the sea. His departure marked the end of the age of divine direct intervention in the world, leaving humanity with the knowledge he had given them.

lore.syncretism: Sukunahikona overlaps with healing deities, sake-brewing kami, and the folklore of tiny spiritual beings. His partnership with Ōkuninushi mirrors other divine helper figures across Eurasia, but his specific role as a healer and brewer is distinctively Japanese.
lore.culturalLegacy: Sukunahikona is venerated at shrines associated with healing and sake brewing. His story remains a favorite in retellings of Japanese myth, and his image as a tiny but mighty deity resonates in a culture that values subtle strength.
lore.extendedMeditation: Sukunahikona teaches that smallness is not weakness. The little prince from across the sea brought medicine, sake, and order to a troubled land. He is the patron of those whose power is underestimated because of their size.
lore.archaeology: Sukunahikona has no major independent archaeological site. His cult is preserved in shrines associated with Ōkuninushi and with healing, as well as in the textual record of the Kojiki.
